utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, can you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Before we start, I just want to place on record our apology for late starting. It was due to unforeseen and urgent personal matters for one of the Judges. I hope we can make up the time. I'm told that the Prosecution has a preliminary matter to raise. And before you do so, Madam Hasan, just to place on record also that due to urgent personal matters Judge Orie is not sitting with us today, as he mentioned yesterday. And therefore Judge Fluegge and I have decided to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis of Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Thank you, Madam Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Yesterday during the cross-examination I raised the testimony of Dragomir Keserovic and this is at transcript pages 351543 -- sorry, 35153 to 35154. And after raising this with the witness, I made a comment and I said: "Keserovic says that this order was made on the evening of the 16th of July." After which I immediately moved to another topic with another question. And I wanted to clarify that comment I made because, in fact, Keserovic says in his testimony in this case that he received the verbal -- that he arrived at Crna Rijeka and the night of the 16th, he is certain of that, but that he may have received the order either that evening or the following evening. And it is rather through his testimony documents and other witness testimony that it's our position that the order was received on the evening of 16 July. So rather than saying, "Keserovic says," I should have been more precise and accurate and said, "It's our position that Keserovic received the order on the 16th of July."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Hasan, for that explanation. It's on the record. Do you feel there's any need for you to correct that position with respect to the witness once he comes in?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: It didn't affect the questions that I asked as far as my assessment -- as far as I assessed the transcript so I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you said immediately thereafter you moved on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Apparently the witness didn't comment on your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: No, not on that comment that I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, thank you so much. Then it's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Just one other minor matter. The Defence had tendered into evidence D1046. You will recall that's the 17 July order issued by General Mladic and I had raised that this was already in evidence as P1579 and we've -- both the Defence and Prosecution has taken a look at the documents and agree that it is the same document. So we'd request that we just maintain the P1579 and it might be appropriate to vacate D1046.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does the Defence confirm that? Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. Before we started this morning, we agreed that D1046 be left free and that the document that we used remains under the number under which it had already been used in evidence in this trial. Our colleague told us about this correction in relation to Keserovic, and we are not going to deal with the matter further in our re-direct. And I would like to thank you her for her attitude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Stojanovic. Then the Court will then vacate D1046, and, Mr. Registrar, you are asked to please vacate that number and reserve it for the next Defence Exhibit and then that document will then stay in the record as P1579. Madam Hasan, are you ready to continue with your cross-examination once the witness is in?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May the witness please be brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness, I just want the record to show that the accused is not with us today as a result of an order that was made yesterday afternoon just before we adjourned for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trkulja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that you're still bound by the oath, the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. Understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Hasan will proceed with her cross-examination. Thank you, Madam Hasan.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trkulja.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You testified yesterday, both in direct and cross-examination, that when you had arrived in Zvornik in the area of Baljkovica that there had not been a break through, that the front line had not broken through, that Obrenovic had told you there had been fighting at the front of Crni Vrh but that he managed to push back the enemy. And I'm referring to transcript pages 35100 and 35103. And that it was the following day, so you arrive on the 17th, and on the 18th, that is when the column, the Muslims who you say were in a ditch, were passing through. And at transcript 35144, lines 6 to 9, you testified you had no idea there was a column, no idea, and then you later told us that Sladojevic was wrong when he said he knew before, when he left Crna Rijeka, that the Muslims had broken through the lines. And I'd like to take you to a 15 July 1995 interim combat report from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And this is 65 ter 4137. If we could have that displayed.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you will see that this is a report from Krstic ...

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we turn briefly in the English to the second page so we can see the stamp. The document was received at 1945 hours and processed at 2010 hours. Now, this interim combat report - and we can revert back to page 1 in the English - is to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I'm just going to read to you just the second paragraph: "At about 0440 hours on 15 July ... the enemy started a heavy artillery attack on the 4th, 6th and 7th Infantry Battalion line of defence. "The attack was carried out at about 0530 hours, but the enemy continued with short intervals of artillery and infantry fire. Three soldiers were wounded in these attacks." I'm going to skip down to the next paragraph: "During the transport towards Zvornik, the Turkish forces pulling out from Srebrenica towards Tuzla in the Planinica village sector opened fire on an ambulance and killed the driver Milos Tesic and paramedic Nenad Stevic." It goes on in the last major paragraph there: "The units are carrying out the blockade and destruction of Muslim forces which are pulling out of Srebrenica towards Tuzla." Now you were at the Main Staff on the evening of the 15th of July, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So you would have received and reviewed this report that came in from General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, in fact, on the night of the 15th, you were aware that there was -- there were Muslim forces moving in the direction of Tuzla; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And contrary to what you had said, which was nobody was blocking, nobody forbid the Muslim formations to exit in the direction of Tuzla, which you said at transcript page 35156 to -- line 25, to 35157, line 2, in fact, the forces -- the Muslim forces were not free to pass to Bosnian-held territory. As Krstic says, they were blocking them and destroying them; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, that is put in very general terms. First of all, these were groups. It wasn't one axis. I gave my statement only about the axis towards Crni Vrh because I'm not aware of any others. I don't know them. Secondly, all of what I said pertained to that group that was moving towards Crni Vrh where I was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I think what you testified to before is clear so let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd offer 65 ter 04137 into evidence. 04137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 04137 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7370, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: All right. So I'm going to turn now to 65 ter 04040.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And what this is, is the Main Staff report that's dated the 15th of July that went to the president of Republika Srpska, amongst others. So we're still on the same night, the night of the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if I could ask that we turn to page 4 in the English and B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You drafted this report; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, if we turn to page 3 in the English and the B/C/S, under item 6 in the zone of the Drina Corps, a, where there's a summary of the enemy, and midway through the paragraph, and this is your drafting, you say: "Their objective is to" -- sorry, I'll start a bit earlier. "The remainder of the scattered Muslim formations from the former Srebrenica enclave are moving towards Kravica and Konjevic Polje. Their objective is to continue breaking through to Mount Udrc and from there to Tuzla and Zivinice. During the course of today's day, several enemy groups have surrendered to VRS members. In the zone of the Zvornik pbr, around 0440 hours, the enemy launched a strong artillery attack on the defence line of the 4th, 6th and 7th Infantry Battalion. The attack ended around 0530 hours, but the enemy continued opening artillery and small-arms fire at short intervals." And then you go on to talk about Turkish troops pulling out from Srebrenica towards Tuzla opening fire on an ambulance in the Planinica village sector, killing the driver of a vehicle and a paramedic. This is the information that you got from Krstic's report we just looked at; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And under "Situation in the corps," item b, you go on to say: "The 1st Zvornik pbr with its reinforcements is carrying out preparations to cut off and encircle enemy soldiers en route from Planinica to Krizevici." Just under "Situation on the territory," Roman numeral II: "The Vlasenica-Zvornik road is unsafe due to the enemy groups from Srebrenica which are trying to breakthrough to Tuzla." So you were reporting to the president and to -- for the information as well, of all the other units listed on this document of what was going on, of the movement of the Muslim forms towards Tuzla, towards Crni Vrh, Mount Udrc and the breakthrough that was expected to take place that -- that you had understood they were attempting to do. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was from the report. I just summarised what had was contained in the report. Now it is the assessment of the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, and you understood that this was his assessment?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. His assessment. Couldn't be mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'd offer 65 ter 04040 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 04040 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7371, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, moving on to 16th July, and I'm still addressing the comment -- the testimony you gave yesterday that you had no idea what was going on when you left for Zvornik and that you didn't know there was a column and that there was no breakthrough. Now you will recall that Defence counsel showed you a report that -- the interim combat report from Pandurevic that was dated the 16th of July. This is P1513. You recall that report?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw and read that report in 2007 when the gentleman there, the Prosecutor, showed it to me. Until then, I hadn't seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you do recall the report, don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall the report but I'm telling when it was that I first saw it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. That was the question: Do you recall the report? "Yes" is a sufficient answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And this is the report that you said never reached you at the Main Staff, and this is at transcript page 35087, starting at line 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And just to refresh everyone's recollection, if we could pull up that document, P1513. And Mr. Stojanovic did read parts of this document. So just as a reminder, it talks about the enemy has continued intensive attacks on the brigade's area along the entire front line with particular intensity in the defence area of the 7th, 4th, 6th, and 3rd Infantry Battalion. He goes on to describe that forces, Muslim forces, "fired almost 1.000 projectiles of varying calibre and that parts of Srebrenica 28th Infantry Battalion, together with previously infiltrated groups, carried out a synchronized Kamikaze attack against the 4th pb, our positions, weapons, and other equipment from the Planinci and Potocari areas, using their numerical advantage, they surrounded the 4th pb. Counting soldiers and civilians, armed and unarmed, all together 7.000." Then he goes on to describe and I believe also Mr. Stojanovic read this part about them capturing the 76-millimetre self-propelled guns and seizing three of the VRS's trenches. And he reports: "The brigade's problem is that part of our forces is surrounded in the Baljkovica area. The enemy has suffered major losses, hundreds of dead, but that has not prevented them from carrying out their intentions." And at the very last paragraph -- sorry, under item 3, this is where Pandurevic provides a justification for opening a corridor, and he says: "In view of the great pressure on the brigade's area of responsibility, the losses sustained, the inability of the surrounded forces to hold out for long, the abandonment of the Zvornik pbr command to deal as best ... it could with the Srebrenica Turks, coupled with the absolute determination of the Turks to save at least some lives, regardless of the losses and in order to prevent losses in our own ranks, I have decided, in view of the situation, to open a corridor ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now I'm going to go to D1045. And, Mr. Trkulja, this is -- this is a report you were also shown and it's the 16th July report that was sent to the president of the RS, among others, and we examined this report as well during your direct examination. And you testified that you drafted this report and it bears your initials at the end of it, NT.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And I'd like it turn to page 4 in the English and 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Under number 6 where there's a report on the Drina Corps zone of responsibility, item a, this is your drafting, sir: "On the Tuzla-Zvornik axis, the enemy regrouped large forces in front of the 1st Zvornik pbr and used them early in the morning in a strong artillery and infantry attack on our units' sector along the Baljkovica-Rijeka-Pandurici axis. They were co-ordinating with ... forces pulling out from the former Srebrenica enclave. They were able to breakthrough the defence and capture three trenches in the Baljkovica village sector, create a corridor for the pullout of civilian population, which was used by about 7.000 mainly unarmed civilians (men, women, children). During this attack, the enemy attacked our units from behind the lines, irrespective of own losses. Thus they captured three self-propelled guns by bodies - losing hundreds of soldiers. We are currently negotiating with the Muslims with regard to freeing the captured policemen and Zvornik Battalion members and the duration of the corridor." Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Hasan, it is really Zvornik Battalion or Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Brigade, I'm sorry. Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, by the time you sat down to draft this report on the night of the 16th of July, and this is before you leave to Baljkovica, you had already received the information contained in Vinko Pandurevic's report. You had received that from the Drina Corps, and this is why it appears here in this report to the president?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partly, yes, because I went towards Crni Vrh and everything I spoke about pertains to Crni Vrh. Had there been more groups, more axes or breakthrough, there were. But I didn't explain any other axis. I was not present. I don't know. That can only be concluded on the basis of the report. I spoke about the place where I was myself, and that is Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's get the story straight because you testified yesterday that you were present at the Main Staff on the 16th of July in Crna Rijeka and that you only left to Zvornik on the 17th of July. This report you drafted on the night of the 16th. So are you telling us that you were in the field on the 16th of July as well?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not in the field. I went on a field mission in the morning, on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So when you just testify, "yes, because I went towards Crni Vrh and everything I spoke about pertains to Crni Vrh," well, you hadn't gone to Crni Vrh yet to include this information in this report. That only happened after you drafted this report.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened one day after this report.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So the information that we see here in this report that's drafted -- you drafted the night of the 16th, is information you received from the Drina Corps and it is based on the information provided by Vinko Pandurevic in his interim combat report dated the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was used was the Drina Corps report. I never saw Pandurevic's report at the command post. I first saw it when I arrived here.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The issue really is that this report does not contain any observations you may have made in Crni Vrh on the 17th, because the report was written before the 17th, irrespective of whether you -- the report is from the Drina Corps or from Pandurevic's report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's precisely the case. We did not have any information as to what was going on at Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, Mr. Trkulja, to be very clear, the Drina -- you had seen a report from the Drina Corps which included the information that is provided in your report that you drafted to the president and which reflects the information Vinko Pandurevic provided in his interim combat report?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Hasan ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Hasan, how much more do you still need? You've reached the end of your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I did not hear you very well. I don't think your microphone was on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I said, according to the Registrar, you have reached the end of your time. How much more time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I actually do think I will need 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Try to squeeze it into 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Very quickly, if we can -- given that you keep mentioning Crni Vrh, if we could look at P1087. This is the Srebrenica map book.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if I could ask for the ERN page that ends 7949, please. Page 19 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you will see on the right border there --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I mean, if we could just zoom into the centre portion of this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You see there's Karakaj and if we just there, by that red and black line, the border there. And if we take a look at -- you see Zvornik there towards the bottom of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And if we go to the left, take a look at the left of that map, okay, and scroll a little bit up. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You see those arrows, that's the movement of the Muslim formations. And just under the date there, 16 July 1995, Mr. Trkulja, do you see Planinci that we keep referring to? Do you see that there?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And you see just to the left of that, where it says "Crni Vrh"?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, in fact, Crni Vrh is just along where the Muslim formations are moving near to -- to the lines there. That's the -- that's the axis of movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What is your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Do you agree, Mr. Trkulja, that your references to Crni Vrh are -- in fact Crni Vrh falls just along the line, the movement of the Muslim formations and their movement up towards the front lines?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, the line that depicts the movement of Muslim forces is an imaginary line. It was just a forecast. One of the groups, possibly the biggest group, was actually moving towards Crni Vrh and not in the direction pointed by the arrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's move on to other things, Mr. Trkulja. Now, you testified that -- at transcript page 35150, lines 1 to 6, that when you arrived in Baljkovica on 17th of July, that the Muslims were in a ditch and that it was only on the 18th of July that they passed through by agreement. You recall your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It is the truth, and there's no two ways around it.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So let's look at P724, please. This is a report submitted by Ljubisa Borovcanin and it's dated 5 September 1995. And he reports on the combat engagement of the special police brigade and other police forces in Operation Srebrenica 95 in the period from 11 to 21 July 1995. And if we turn to page 4 in the English and B/C/S, please, he provides an account of what happened on the 16th of July. And he says: "Today, there was fierce fighting with the Muslim forces in the areas of Krizevici, Tisova Kosa, and Baljkovica. The Muslim attack" -- and he goes on to say: "The Muslim attack was very fierce and was backed by artillery from Nezuk. In the morning, the enemy captured 57-millimetre self-propelled guns from members of the Army of Republika Srpska which protected the left flank of the MUP forces. Because of this, the situation changed dramatically. From a distance of 400 to 500 metres, these self-propelled guns directly pounded our hardware, vehicles, ambulances, and the communications centre." And then he goes on to say: "There was danger that our forces would be completely cut off and surrounded." And the last sentence: "The Army of Republika Srpska had about 40 killed and more than 80 wounded. It was not possible to establish the exact number immediately. "At about 1500 hours" -- if we can turn now to page 5 in the B/C/S: "The bulk of the enemy column (about 2.500 soldiers) managed to breakthrough to Nezuk." If we turn to page 5 in the English, Borovcanin continues to say that: "At 1300 hours," and this is the 16th of July, "the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Vinko Pandurevic, and the commander of the Muslim side, Semso Muminovic, agreed to open a 1-kilometre wide corridor in the areas of Parlog and Baljkovica to allow all the Muslim soldiers to get out."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You see that there? Now --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a map before me.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I don't think there's a need for a map at this point in time. Now, so when you arrived on the 17th of July, what Borovcanin reports here had already transpired the day before; right?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but on a different axis. Not on the one where I was. Baljkovica is not even close.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, this is exactly -- Borovcanin is reporting what Pandurevic had also reported in his interim combat report. And if we look, sir, to 17th of July, Borovcanin says that: "In co-ordination with the intervention units of the Zvornik Brigade, the 5th Special Police Detachment closed the line in Baljkovica and combed the area towards Crni Vrh." So you had told us that you arrived on the 17th and that on the 18th the corridor was opened and it was closed on the 18th and then you left back to -- to Crna Rijeka. Well, in fact, sir, you arrived on the 17th and then that is when the -- the corridor had already been opened the day before, and it was on the 17th of July, the day that you arrived, that it was closed. So you've got your chronology wrong. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not the case. My chronology is absolutely correct. You found a report where the duty officer recorded when I arrived Zvornik, when I left, and I told you exactly who was present. I told you that at 10.00 on the 18th, they started withdrawing, and that's correct. And now, for the fact that some people are lost in time and space, well, that's their problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: And, sir, the day -- and let's leave aside the date. But the day that you watched -- that you were present when the corridor was closed, Vinko Pandurevic was with you. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw him in the morning on the 18th when Muslim forces were supposed to start withdrawing. There were a lot of officers in the evening as well but I can't remember that he was there. My memory doesn't serve me well in that respect. On the 17th, he was there and he issued an order in that part of the front line. The Zvornik Brigade had a huge front line, some 20 or 30 kilometres long. The road between Zvornik and Vlasenica was not safe. So there were all sorts of possibilities. I'm just telling you that in my statement everything is about what was going around Crni Vrh. There were no MUP forces there is at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Trkulja, could you please slow down when you speak because the interpreters are desperately trying to keep pace with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Now, surely Pandurevic must have briefed you on what happened. And you've told what you say Obrenovic had told you -- told you. But what did Pandurevic tell you?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pandurevic didn't tell me a thing. I saw him in the morning. We greeted each other. And we allowed the events to take their course, as had been agreed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Hasan, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will have a few more questions after the break, if you will allow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My colleague has just reminded me that Mr. Mladic is not here, so we can go for another 30 minutes before we take the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So, Witness, you are there to -- with two other colonels from the Main Staff, Sladojevic and Stankovic. And you do not receive any information from Pandurevic about what is happening there? You're sent by the Main Staff and you don't inquire about a corridor that was opened which you knew about?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A correction. Colonel Stankovic was not with me. There was a major whose name I can't remember, a member of the Drina Corps. I didn't know what the situation at Crni Vrh was. Not even the duty officer with whom the major had spoken knew. If he had known, if somebody had told us, we would have never gone there.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sir, now, you had said that you were sent off with Sladojevic and Stankovic, and the order that we saw from the 17th of July --

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whom?

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Sladojevic, Bogdan Sladojevic. And Stankovic, Milovan Stankovic. He was the chief of reconnaissance, sabotage in the intelligence administration of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was there, as a matter of fact, but he didn't go with us. You can read that in the telegram. But he never joined us. He didn't go with us because we never complied with that telegram. I went with Sladojevic and with the major that I mentioned, the one from the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 26085, please. And this is the OTP's interview of Sladojevic some 15 years ago in October 2000. And he describes what Pandurevic said. If we could get page 4 in the B/C/S. It's around line 24. And the same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're looking for the page, can you repeat the number of the 65 ter number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 26085.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can we turn one page in the English, please. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: So he says and you can see it in the -- in your language at line -- around line 24. In the English we're looking at approximately line 8. So he says -- I'll just start a bit higher. He asked: "Where is the commander, what's going on here? The commander came maybe five minutes later, he didn't introduce himself but I drew a conclusion that that was Lieutenant-Colonel Vinko Pandurevic. And he just briefly showed on which position Muslim artillery fired the day before."

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: If we could turn now the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: He goes on to say: "There was a kind of an orchard with plum trees and the forest and everything was scratched there. They said that they attacked from the front and also from the rear and that lasted for about two hours. It all happened the day before. He said that he had 49 dead, 68 seriously wounded. I know that approximately he said that 120 of his people were incapacitated. 20 minutes later, Lieutenant-Colonel Obrenovic came who was at the time [sic] I think Chief of Staff. When he came, he showed -- he pointed at the self-propelled gun where these people form the column confiscated their machine-gun and their gun inflicted losses. The column went towards Kladanj and Kalesija. Vinko said that he managed to get in touch with the Muslim commander, he had contact -- that they exchanged the dead bodies and Stankovic asked him if he had any indication there will be another attack, attempt to take over Zvornik. He said that there were no indications." And he goes on. Now, sir, that's indeed what Pandurevic and Obrenovic reported to you that day, on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late Mr. Sladojevic's statement is completely incorrect. He just got lost in time and space. On the 17th, in the evening, it was Obrenovic who reported to us. He showed us the lines and everything else. He explained what had been agreed with regard to opening the front line. If he didn't speak to him privately, not officially, while we were waiting for Muslim forces to pass through, there was nothing official. There was no official report. The military part was nothing that Pandurevic did on the 18th in the morning. Pandurevic was merely present there. Now, as to whether he had a private chat with Sladojevic, I don't know. I was the leader of that group, and if there was anything relevant, he would have spoken to me. Secondly, Obrenovic did not know whether there were casualties or how many. I mean, he didn't know that in the evening on the 17th. At 10.00 they started coming out. You can read that everywhere. And now he mentions a totally different time. That's why I say that he was lost in time and space. They started leaving on the 10th, they finished at 12.00, and then we left. And yesterday we spoke about the sanitisation process, but that is a matter for the organs of the rear, not the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Mr. Trkulja, do you know of any other incident during the Bosnian war where VRS sustained the number of casualties referred to here in such a short period of time? Are you aware of any such instance?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was several. On Ozren, on Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: But you would agree, Mr. Trkulja, that the number -- these -- these figures were significant losses for the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: You accepted, didn't you, that it was military necessity that drove Vinko Pandurevic to withdraw and to reach an agreement with the Muslims so that he could save the lives of his soldiers?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same question was put last time. But I don't agree with that. They were there with three tanks. Our late Sladojevic forgot to say that. They used three tanks to push the Muslim forces to the ditch. Pandurevic, had he wanted to destroy them, he would have done that within two hours and nobody would have survived. They didn't have the anti-armour resources to defend themselves. They were sitting ducks, if you will. Pandurevic decided to painlessly deal with the situation, to let them leave, and he got two platoons from the positions on the 17th in the evening. All of this is incorrect. All of this you have here is incorrect. On the 17th in the evening, he ordered those two platoons to do that and they left. That's the truth. You see, 700 is mentioned and that's when we had breakfast at the monastery. I didn't want to offend anyone, but I did say that he was lost in time and space. And then --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the last sentence, sir. Can you mention the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We started getting out at 10.00. It all ended at 12 and we left. I mean, I and my team. I and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Hasan, please control your witness to keep it to the tight schedule. You have gone beyond your 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'll just end with one final question, if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: When you returned to Crna Rijeka, you reported to Miletic, you said. What did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just told him everything I said to you just now. The journey to Srebrenica, they weren't there, they went around in a circle, then went to see the duty officer and --

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I'm interested in what you reported to him in response to your -- the mission that you were sent on, what did you tell him about that? Not about your excursion to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: NEDELJKO TRKULJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: About that task, actually it turned out completely different since the Muslim forces had passed through -- actually, that the front line was re-established. I mean, I described to him what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: I have nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Hasan. This may be an appropriate time to take the break. Sir, we'll take a break of 30 minutes. Could you please be back in court at quarter past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since I won't have any questions for Colonel Trkulja and if the Trial Chamber will not have any questions, perhaps this would be the right moment to thank Colonel Trkulja. If you have questions, of course, it's an entirely different matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Stojanovic, for mentioning that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Trkulja, Mr. Stojanovic just indicated that he has no further questions to you. The Bench also hasn't got any further questions for you so this brings us to the end of your testimony. I take this opportunity to thank you for coming all the way to come and testify and answer all the questions put to you by both parties and the Bench. You are now excused. You may follow the usher. Travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at quarter past 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we continue, I just place it on the record that Mr. Mladic has joined us in court today now. Mr. Stojanovic, or Mr. Ivetic, are we ready to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours. The Defence would call Tihomir Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May the witness please be brought into court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Rules require that before you give your testimony you must make a declaration, a copy of which is being handed over to you. Would you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic is counsel for Mr. Mladic, and he's standing to your left. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would like to first ask you to set forth your full name for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Tihomir Stevanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, could you also tell us where and when you were born.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 20th of January, 1950, in the village of Lijesanj, in Zvornik, Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, have you testified as a witness in the courtroom in any other legal proceedings before today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You mean before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In any court?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In any court, yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in a situation to testify in a misdemeanours court in my place of residence. I did not testify here. However, I was announced as a witness for Radivoje Miletic. I stayed here for nine days and for justified personal reasons, I gave a statement and went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you briefly detail for us your civilian educational background, first of all.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary school in my place of birth, the village of Lijesanj and Drinjaca combined, four plus four, because there weren't eight grades in Lijesanj. Then I graduated from the secondary military school in Belgrade. It's a four-year school. Communications, that what's I studied. Then I completed a course from 1970 -- no, 1980 -- no, 1976, for encoding, at the school centre for communications in Belgrade. In 1987, I graduated from the Military Academy. I studied part-time, and I completed a school for encoders. It was a nine-month course.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could just tell us how long the course in encoding lasted or [B/C/S spoken] I think is the words you used?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first training as an organ for cryptographic data protection that only pertained to NCOs of the former JNA lasted three months, and I was trained for encoding and partial encryption and decryption of encoded telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in relation to your time in the military, can you briefly chronicle for us the positions and ranks that you held at various times during your professional career up to the outbreak of the war in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I graduated from a school for NCOs with top marks, I was entitled to choose where I would serve and I chose Bijeljina. As a sergeant I was a squad leader. In 1972 I went to Sarajevo, to the garrison there, and I was commander of a platoon in the 7th Army. In 1987, when I received my commission, I worked in the communications organ of the 7th Army for three years. And then I was transferred to the 4th Battalion of communications at the Lukavica barracks as company commander. I carried out those duties until operations started. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you say when operations started. What specific post did you hold at the time the war in the former Yugoslavia started?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: When the war started in the former Yugoslavia, I was commander of the 2nd Mixed Company at the 4th Battalion for communications at the Lukavica garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And where were you living and where was your family living when the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: My family lived in Sarajevo, in the neighbourhood of Ciglane.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did your family remain living there when the war broke out in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: We have to go back to 1991, when my older son went to the JNA, and my younger son and my wife stayed on in Sarajevo, until it broke out -- actually, until possibilities were created for leaving Sarajevo because it was critical. It was hard to stay there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What made it hard to stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get a time-frame?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what time-frame are you talking about, first of all?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the end of March, beginning of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then could you give us some idea of what you mean when you say: "... it was critical. It was hard to stay there"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, already at that time, in 1991, the leadership of the SDA there, then-president Alija Izetbegovic, something was issued that was not an order, it was a suggestion, not to serve in the JNA. Part of the Serb population in Sarajevo did not accept that, and we sent our children to do their military service. The Muslims didn't do that, but it wasn't all of them. Some still went to do their military service. Those who accepted call-up papers and sent their children to do their military service were not well liked in Sarajevo, and they were exposed to provocations, including myself and my family. We were exposed to that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And where did your family go?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: My family, that is to say, my son and my wife who stayed on -- first my son left through Butmir airport, went to Belgrade. And my wife moved from Ciglane where we had lived and where she was seriously taunted because I moved to the barracks because of the heightened alert. She moved to Grbavica. And there was another lady there, the wife of my colleague, and together with her she went to Rajlovac and again through the airport she went to Belgrade and then from there to Zrenjanin and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to join the Army of Republika Srpska, and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I was in the 4th Battalion for communications of the 4th Corps, I was already in the Lukavica barracks. Immediately when the 2nd Military District left the barracks on the square of the 6th of April, around the 6th of May, on orders, I established a unit that was reinforced from the 1st Company and from my own company, manpower and equipment included, left -- so we left Sarajevo with a column and soldiers to the Tvrdimici neighbourhood where I established a communications centre at the command post of the then-4th Corps. Immediately after the centre was established, the corps commander, General Vojislav Djurdjevac arrived. In this way I automatically joined the Army of Republika Srpska, although it wasn't called the Army of Republika Srpska at that time. Because my unit was a mixed unit. Officially, as for the Army of Republika Srpska, I joined on the 19th of May, the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say your unit was a mixed unit, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's simple. In my unit, I then had mixed ethnic backgrounds, Serbs, Macedonians, Hungarians, who were from different republics; Macedonia, Serbia, and Montenegro. At the time while I was at Tvrdimici I didn't have any Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during this time-period, did you have knowledge of the withdrawal of other JNA personnel from the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Again we have to go back to the Lukavica barracks and link that to my stay in the Lukavica barracks. Because I was a member of the communications battalion of the 4th Corps, one of the tasks of my units was following the withdrawal of units from the Sarajevo garrison and the transfer to Serb-controlled territory -- or actually not that, it was safer at the time, safer territory. And that was the Lukavica garrison. So I was in a position to follow the withdrawal of the column from Zenica with General Sipcic, who was a colonel then, then the Marsal Tito barracks, then the auto battalion from Alipasa's bridge and the command of the 2nd Military District from the 6th April Square in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe for us by what means were you able to follow with -- the withdrawal of these units that have you identified for us.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the truth. At that time, when units were withdrawing, JNA units were withdrawing from garrisons, the ones that I already mentioned, I think the reason is already well known, because they were exposed to constant attacks and there was a high degree of intolerance, so they couldn't stay on in these settings. So we communicated with these units and we regulated the following. We used RUP-12s and PRCs that had the same capabilities and they were in the so-called small staff command vehicles and units had these resources. At the head in the back of the column, they had such equipment and such vehicles. And we, from the Lukavica barracks, followed their departure, their march, and their arrival at the Lukavica garrison, which was their destination. I can add that Miroslav Micic, who was then a sergeant, worked on these communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the course of the withdrawal of the various units or -- or formations that you said you were involved in following, did you recall any problems or incidents that arose in relation to the same?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, there's one thing I didn't say, and that is that we followed the withdrawal of the military police battalion from the Viktor Bubanj barracks so that's included too. I do remember. Let us start with the auto battalion that was at Alipasino Polje, no Most, Alipasin Most. When the column set out, it was sometime in the morning. We had communication with the front end and the back of that column. However, immediately as soon as they were supposed to set out, there were certain problems because part of the Muslim forces called the Green Berets tried to infiltrate the column and to cut it in two and that was prevented at the very outset. The column continued its March from Alipasin Most to Lukavica. However, soon after they left the barracks compound, again the unit was -- or, rather, the column was cut in two because we lost communication with the back of the column. The personnel at the back of the column, in this vehicle for communication, pointed out to us that it's possible that it was cut in two, the column, which proved to be true. In half an hour or 40 minutes, the head of the column and that half of the column that had left Alipasin Most arrived, and then they were directed to Sarajevo -- or, rather, the Green Berets took those vehicles, seized them, the ones that we never got back. That goes for that barracks. As for the Marsal Tito barracks, that was the centre for training infantry recruits with a complete infrastructure, and everything else that is required by institutions of higher learning of a military nature. There were no problems with withdrawal there, and the unit left without any problems and went on to Belgrade. Of course, the -- the personnel there were of mixed backgrounds and I don't know what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, that was a real long and very detailed answer, and the previous answers were also quite long. You indicated, first, that you would need for examination-in-chief one and a half hours. You increased the time for two hours. Is it because you realised that the witness is giving detailed answers far beyond some of the questions you have put to him? Or what is the reason for that? I --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The reason was additional information that was not known to me, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- that was a part of the proofing note, that I then have additional questions to ask the witness, additional areas to explore with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. But at the moment we are dealing with matters which are -- were dealt with in some detail with previous witnesses. You should try to keep it short and not to -- to make sure that the witness is really focusing on your questions and not expanding too much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will endeavour to do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, was there any other of the withdrawals that resulted in any incidents or problems that you have knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, I'll keep it short, no problem. The Viktor Bubanj barracks, there were no problems in the withdrawal of the personnel there. One should not ignore the case of the murder of a soldier in the barracks before the troops' departure. There was, however, a lot of problems in another area. The problems were of the same nature as those when the Alipasin Most barracks were being closed and the troops withdrawing from there. There were casualties there and you know about that already. Those casualties were on the side of the withdrawing unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which unit was withdrawing because that has not come into our transcript? Which -- the withdrawal of which unit or entity are you speaking of where there were casualties?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The command of the 2nd Military District was withdrawing. The officers and the accompanying soldiers or escorts who worked within the facility or provided services for the command. I'm talking about the command of the 2nd Military District, they were withdrawing. They were headed by General Kukanjac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, either during your time as a JNA officer or afterwards when you became a VRS officer, did you have occasion to have some information or insight into the placement of ABiH military forces or installations within the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Can we get a time-frame? That's so broad that -- given the information we have that he's been all over the place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Subsequent to March of 1992, did you occasion to have some information or insight into the placement of ABiH military forces or installations within the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: As all the other officers of the VRS, I did have certain information about the locations of their forces or at least some of their forces. In view of the fact that the barracks had been abandoned on the 6th of April, the barracks in Bascarsija, that's where I had been in service, the Marsal Tito barracks --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt but the question was answered and now we're going off into a narrative. He did have information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have information of any locations of a civilian nature where the Army BiH had military troops or installations located?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that's a leading question, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have direct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just a second, sir. Just a second, Mr. Witness. I think that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, my prior question was open-ended and he started giving an answer and I had objection from the other side, so they wanted me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Nobody [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's no justification for giving a leading question next. You still have to ask a non-leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where there were locations might -- has not been asked yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At the risk of opening up a narrative, where were their locations located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, one of the brigades, according to the information of our security organ. I can give you his name, Colonel Milorad Bukva. I also know indirectly that they were also located in the Kosevo hospital, the military hospital. That's where they opened fire from. There was some individual locations in the tunnel, in the brick-works. That's where they had heavy weaponry and they opened fire from it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You have identified the Kosevo hospital and the military hospital as places where the ABiH opened fire from. What is the basis of that knowledge or information that you have?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That man, who is my relative, still lives in Sarajevo. I need to protect him. He was in Sarajevo throughout the war and he was treated at Kosevo hospital and then in military hospital. He told me that, for example, in the military hospital, fire was opened from the balcony. Mortar fire was opened from there. And the patients were sheltered in the basement because they knew that there would be retaliation, that fire would be returned. They opened fire from the Kosevo hospital, from the park, because the hospital is surrounded by greenery. They entered the hospital's perimeter and they opened fire from there. Also in view of the fact that person resided in the military field in Djordje Andrejevic Kun Street, leaning on Nedzarici, that's where our unit was, and the settlement was called Vojnicko Polje. Often heavy weaponry would be brought by the police commanded by Vikic and fire was opened from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection -- objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He's asked for the basis or the knowledge and we have apparently a friend who he doesn't want to name and now he has just gone into a narrative without any basis. And you know, we've been here a long time, to be getting unnamed, second- and third-hand sources, if he is serious about this, we can go into private session. But to me this is -- has very little probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would be happy to go into private session with Your Honours' leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We are now in open session, Mr. Stevanovic, so be careful what you say now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one question to the witness, please. You mentioned a relative of yours. Is that the only source of your knowledge in the information you gave earlier about location of ABiH forces in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you more about that, but I can see that you will not allow me to expand. In view of the nature of my work that I carried out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I would like to interrupt you. I asked you if he is the only source. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What other sources do you base your knowledge on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My personal knowledge and the knowledge of the security organs of my unit, and by that, I mean the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to the departure of civilians from parts of the city of Sarajevo which were not controlled by the JNA or the VRS?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the war; i.e., when the security situation became tense, my family and myself and then all of my friends and later a lot of other people left Pofalici. Pofalici was under a lot of pressure and under that pressure the people caved in and they abandoned the neighbourhood. I saw that personally some of those men joined my unit in Trebevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Let's break this down. Tell us what part you saw personally of what was going on in Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Between 8.00 and 9.00 in the morning, and I don't remember the date, it was a long time ago, right? The Pofalici settlement, where 80 to 85 per cent of the population were Serbs, came under an attack and you could see that with the naked eye from the command of the 4th Corps where I was at the time. You could also observe the situation through the binoculars. You could observe the situation better through binoculars. There was an attack and then the houses were torched and those houses and facilities were property of the Serbs. And then people started arriving in the territory of Vogosca, Ilidza, Lukavica, Tilava. All those areas were controlled by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now who was attacking the settlement of Pofalici that you observed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now earlier you also said "some of those men joined my unit in Trebevic." Who was it that later joined your unit in Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, sir, not Trebevic but Tvrdimici. My unit was in the village of Tvrdimici. That's where the command post was as well. Those were mostly drivers by trade, common folks, who were militarily able-bodied. My unit was a special unit and the only people who could join it were communications men and drivers. There were some communications guys, not many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: But from where did they men come to join you at Tvrdimici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the settlement of Pofalici.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: They were assigned to my unit, in practical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you earlier also mentioned -- you said something about Bascarsija. What was in Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Above Bascarsija - and Bascarsija is about 100 to 150 metres as the crow flies from the Jajce barracks where I had served for 14 years - their battalion of military police was billeted there. And since you could see that area from the area controlled by the Serbs, we suffered daily fire being opened on our positions from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, can you tell us did you remain in the Sarajevo area the entirety of the war or did you transfer to some other unit or formation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: As needed, when the company was fully established and when it was moved together with the command post from the village of Tvrdimici to Pale, to the tourist hotel there where the command post of the 4th Corps was, at the beginning of March 1993, on the order of the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS and at the proposal of the communications organ of the Army of Republika Srpska, I was reassigned to Crna Rijeka to the communications regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we continue with the communications regiment, I'm not sure if you identified who was in the barracks at Jajce as the transcript does not record that element. So I would ask for you to please repeat for us who was quartered in the Jajce barracks.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean during the war? During war activities?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The military police of the Muslim military. It was a battalion of the military police. That was their strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, coming back to your transfer to the communications regiment, what were your precise duties within the communications regiment when you first arrived in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try and keep it short. I was appointed as the company commander for the communications garrison. That was in the rank of a communications battalion. That was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long you stayed in this position?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until March 1995. And then I became a member of the communications department of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What rank did you hold at the time that you were appointed to the communications regiment in March of 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Captain first class.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What rank did you have when you joined the communications department of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what specific position did you have at the Department of Communications of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was the desk officer for cryptographic protection in the communications department of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While you were at this position in the communications department of the Main Staff, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: My immediate superior was Colonel Radomir Prole.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now moving backwards to the first position that you held at the Main Staff within the communications regiment, where were you physically located during the time of performance of your duties?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, in order to answer your question, I have to say that the communications company had a relay platoon which was quartered at Veliki Zep. It had a telephone platoon, the ATC platoon, and the maintenance squad. The last three units were quartered at the Goljak 1 feature where I was also quartered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the Goljak 1 feature, what kind of a feature or structure was that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It depended on the unit formations and their changes. First it was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. [In English] The interpreters have asked that you speak more slowly, sir. Could you please restart your answer.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. According to the first and original version, the Goljak 1 structure was intended for the rear command post of the former 7th Army. When that was disbanded, its purpose was to serve as the rear command post of the corps. And when the war broke out, that's where the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska was quartered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what kind of building was Goljak 1?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Goljak 1 was a sub-terrain facility featuring all the necessary equipment for the stay and work of a command, the size of the then-Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It could go on working uninterruptedly for 75 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What can you tell us about the staffing levels that you experienced at the communications regiment when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just like all the other units, the communications regiment was understaffed. It had two battalions. It had a company for garrison communications and a rear platoon. When it comes to my company, it was supposed to have -- I can't remember exactly what it would have been according to establishment, but it should have been 130 men. When I arrived there, I found between 60 and 70 men in the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now going back to your second position that you held after March of 1995, when you were a desk officer for cryptographic protection, could you tell us what were the precise duties that this position entailed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The duties of a desk officer for cryptographic data protection in the Main Staff of the VRS was to organise cryptographic data protection at the level of the VRS, to secure technical equipment and means, as well as all the necessary documents that were needed for the normal functioning of cryptographic data protection at all levels of the VRS. I inherited that position from Lieutenant-Colonel Miroslav Radakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in this position?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the end of the war and then I continued in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. When did you retire from active military service?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What rank did you have at the time of retirement?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you've identified for us Goljak 1. Were there any other buildings or structures that made up the Main Staff facility at -- command facility?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Within the perimeter of Crna Rijeka, there was Goljak 1, the so-called Barake [phoen] settlement. The Veliki Zep feature which was a radio-relay facility. The buildings and commands of the 65th Motorised Regiment and the communications regiment, their commands were in wooden huts, and the troops were in dugouts. There was also the G2, or Goljak 2, feature which was very close but it was not secured and there was nobody there. Within the complex of those features, there was also the Goljak 3 facility, which was located some 7 to 10 kilometres further away, near Han Pogled mountain pass on the Han Pijesak-Vlasenica road.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to tell us what means of communication made up the communications network available to the Main Staff of the VRS at Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can we get a time-frame or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the time-period that you were there, from March of 1993 until the end of the war in 1995, could you give us an overview of the means of communications that were -- that made up the communications network of the Main Staff of the VRS at Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the point of view of the duties that I performed, I have to give the following answer, which is professional. The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska used an integrated system of communications that consisted of radio communications, radio-relay communications, wire communications, and courier communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to break that down a bit, and I would ask you to describe for us which type of radio-relay devices were utilized by the VRS Main Staff for communications with its subordinate corps?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska used the following radio-relay devices that were positioned at Veliki Zep; namely, SMC, RR radio-relay device, RRU, FM-200, RRU-9. RRU-800 not so often. Then RRU-1 which has a single channel. That is what I have to say about radio-relay devices.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Before we continue, Your Honours, I think that we started at 15 after. We're on a different schedule today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, we're trying to configure the hours because we spent one and a half hours this morning, so if we can go until 25 past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, were any of these -- were any of the routes covered by this radio-relay communications equipment you've just identified for us able to carry encrypted communications?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, briefly. That's a brief answer, yes. And I can explain how, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: First of all, which routes could be encrypted?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could have and had to have been encrypted. All of those going to the 1st Corps, the Herzegovina Corps, the Eastern Bosnia Corps, and the air force and air defences, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the Presidency, all of them were encrypted, protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about with the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm sorry, I apologise if I omitted that. It was by accident. Yes, the Drina Corps too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell -- describe for us the types of encryption devices that were in use in relation to the radio-relay communications between the Main Staff and these other parties that you have identified where encrypted communications went?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since these are radio-relay devices and that kind of protection, the two basic devices for cryptography protection of speech that went through these systems is KZU-71 and KZU-61. Let me make a distinction here so that would be clear. The KZU-71 had the possibility of protecting a group of telephone channels, speech channels, transmitted by this system; whereas KZU-61 could protect only one channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about for -- you identified that these are for speech. Were there any encryption devices for written communication?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Cryptographic protection referred to written information and spoken information. For written information there were several systems. The safest and most often used one was R-7. Then 31. They were used for the protection of written information along with T-G4 or, rather, KZU-31.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us, first of all, how the KZU-71 and the KZU-61 devices performed their encryption function?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. This is English, but it's not R-7. It's S-7. I see this in this text although I don't understand English. So now let me go back to the answer. KZU-71 was placed between the radio-relay device and AMD-310. They could have been from -- they could have had four, eight or 32 channels. Usually it was between eight and 16 channels. And all information that was open arrived in KZU-71. And when exiting KZU-71, moving towards a radio-relay device, this information became encrypted. For KZU-71 to secure encryption of information that is arriving, before that it was necessary to carry out certain preparations by inserting a key for encryption or, rather, decryption.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can you to be precise. When you say "a key," what kind of key is that? Is that a physical key?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. This is a coded tape that is put into this key -- no, no, into the device itself. It is read into it, into its electronic system, and it is valid for 15 days up to a month, and I would usually change it every 15 days. That was my practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
