utterances.text: Okay. Could you go on then and complete telling us how the KZU-71 and 61 devices functioned.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this electronic system --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please speak more clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The interpreters have asked that you speak slowly and try to speak more clearly, perhaps with the microphone closer to you, so that they can better follow you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It is not a question of the microphone. Could the witness please speak clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I thought that I was even speaking too loud. So it was open speech that came into KZU-71, and the key that was inserted before that into the electric electronic system, the electronic system of the KZU-71 made it possible to scramble this speech so when leaving that device and then further on through radio relay, it would be transmitted in an encoded way, a single tone, namely, so nothing could be understood. And there could be no decryption or, rather, there couldn't be any interception therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Are there any major differences between the way that the KZU-61 encryption device worked?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, KZU-71 is a more modern piece of communication -- piece of equipment and it enables the kind of communication we have now, whereas 61 is a device that encoded speech. However, it required very slow speech so that it could be transmitted to the other side. Its abilities were modest, in terms of transmission capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did either of these encryption devices need to be activated or turned on in order to function when someone was using a radio-relay device?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: As soon as there is radio-relay communication and as soon as telephone channels get through and as soon as quality is tested, KZU-71 is put in and it works all the time and it does not require any kind of activation at a further point. It is activated throughout. And it reacts to speech, and then speech is encoded afterwards. So it doesn't have to be switched on afterwards. It's on all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we're at the 26-minute mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 1.00. Could you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break at come back at quarter to 1.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness, Mr. Stojanovic, the Chamber received information that the Defence would like to address a scheduling issue for the week 18th to the 22nd of May. I'm not asking that you do that now, just indicate whether -- are you going to do it or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will do that, Your Honour. We expect to be able to do that tomorrow morning, concerning the last working week this month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to these keys for the encryption devices that were changed every 15 to 30 days, where did these keys come from?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I provided those keys to the units.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand whether the witness said that he can or cannot say where the key was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: If necessary, I can say where it was made, and I'm the one who provided them to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could also then tell us where they were manufactured.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The keys for encoding written and spoken information were made at the Institute of Applied Mathematics and Physics in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could somebody with the same radio-relay communications equipment and the same encryption device but without a key for the encryption device listen to the voice communications that were transmitted via such a device?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to radio devices. What radio devices did the VRS Main Staff have at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I was speaking about the communications used by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, I said radio communications as well. The radio communications used by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska were very powerful pieces of equipment and they were used exceptionally, seldom, very rarely. Only in situations when it was absolutely necessary. Also, radio devices that were short-range, Motorolas, were used, as well as radio telephone equipment in the vehicles of the commander and the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. First of all, on what types of occasions would radio devices be exceptionally used?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: If all radio-relay communications with subordinate units were down. That did not happen until our radio-relay facilities were bombed or, rather, our node centres. They were just used for conveying short orders, written information. One kilowatt, RTP, 1 kilowatt - that's the device - they make it possible to encode and decode information and transmit such written information because they include teleprinters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now you also mentioned, I believe, Motorolas and vehicle-based radio equipment. What was the range of the same?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Radio communication in vehicles was only based on repeater links. The range was short and it depended on the configuration of the terrain. So they were not always successful. I can state with responsibility that these communications were used seldom.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to focus for a bit on the types of radio or communications devices that were available to the vehicles that were used by General Mladic. Could you first identify for us who was in charge of setting up and maintaining such equipment in the vehicles of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the technical --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness start again, speaking clearly and slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you please start your answer again and speak more slowly and clearly so that the interpreters can catch every word.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Radio telephone devices that were installed in vehicles that were used by the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska were maintained by professionals from the logistics platoon of the communications regiment of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: These radio telephone devices, based on what technology did they operate? What type were they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Electromagnetic waves. But the range was short. And it depended on repeaters only, their range depended on that, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: On what type of vehicles of General Mladic were these devices installed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: On Puchs. It's a vehicle called Puch.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What type of a vehicle is a Puch?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a terrain vehicle and that's a vehicle that usually commanders had.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What -- what about civilian vehicles that were used by General Mladic at the Main Staff? What type of equipment for communications would those vehicles have?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: In civilian vehicles that were used by General Mladic there was no communications equipment that he could use.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to move to written communications. Could you please first tell us what is the difference between an act and a telegram?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. This word that you used, "ukaz," did you mean "act"?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I meant "act."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Can we have a foundation before we -- I haven't heard these words even used by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is counsel saying he doesn't know what a telegram is? I'm confused by the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Counsel says he hasn't heard the witness talk about act and telegram, and doesn't know what "act" means. Part of the objection is simply that the question is leading and then -- and then you're introducing something that the witness has never talked about. I don't know what an act is because you said first "act," which I thought was an English word, and when you said "act," I didn't know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's take it a step backwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please describe for us the process by which written communications are initiated and sent by one end in the network to another end in the network, telling first what technology and what the steps in the process are.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In order for communication to be transmitted, written information, first of all, that information has to be typed up on a typewriter on an A4 piece of paper. That information has to bear a letterhead, a heading, brief text, the address of the addressee, the addressee, then written text from which one is supposed to see what one wishes to have done by way of this information. At the end of the text, there has to be -- there have to be the initials of the person who processed this; namely, the person who typed this, then a signature, and a stamp. Such a document is packed in an envelope, is sent by courier in a locked bag to the facility number 1. It is handed over to the encoder. The encoder takes over the document, sees who it is addressed to, places his own stamp there, sending stamp, and records the time when the document was received at the encoding station. Then the telegram is encoded, using a certain encoding system. Then the time is registered as to when the telegram was encoded, and then there is a tape that comes out of the teleprinter within this system. Then, according to the log-book there, it is sent to the teleprinter station, and then it is sent to the address that is noted there. Once the teleprinter operator receives confirmation of receipt, such a telegram -- receipt of such a telegram, then information is provided to the encoder. Then on the sending stamp, the time of receipt is recorded. The document is placed in an envelope and, again, through a courier, it is returned to the person or organ that had sent it. The tape is guarded for 24 hours, the encryption tape. If he doesn't receive a request for repetition, the encryption tape and the key that had been used to encode that telegram is destroyed by fire. That completes the telegram-sending process.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go back to the original that has to have a stamp, a signature, and then is sent by a locked courier bag to the encoder to be encoded and sent to the receiver, what is the name in the military parlance of that type of document, the original?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: A document, an enactment.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: May I be allowed to explain that?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: If a document was processed and intended for sending by telegram, all the data it contains are on the left-hand side. The person who drafted the document, a short content, who dictated, who typed it, a signature, and a stamp, a round stamp, all that is on the left-hand side. A document which is intended for courier dispatch, i.e., a document that is to be personally delivered to the recipient, is signed on the right-hand side. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just for my own clarification, I keep hearing the witness talking of "act."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which of these words that are on the transcript here is the equivalent of "act."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it would be better for the translators to perhaps answer that question so I'm not giving evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what an act is? Let the interpreters interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Written information typed up, original, not encoded, without any cryptographic data protection. That's a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the -- what is received on the other end and what is processed and decoded, what is the name for that recipient's copy of the written communication?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will use the kind of terminology that exists both in the military and civilian structure. It is a received telegram or an incoming telegram. The coder has to decode it to turn it back into its original telegram form, the incoming telegram, that is. If necessary, I can explain the whole procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me see if I can work through some parts first. Once the original act has been presented for transmission to the encryptions officer, can that encryptions officer change any of the text in that original act before sending it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: A decoder is forbidden from changing anything in the original text. He can't even delete a comma or a full stop or a single letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, you've described for us this tape that comes out of the teleprinter. How does that tape function on both ends; that is, on the encoding and on the decoding side?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: For a telegram to be encrypted or encoded there's a key and there is an open text. First you draft a text and then there is a reader of a special cryptographic machine, a tape of the open text is placed there, and then there is a second reader where you place a key tape also [indiscernible]. As a product you receive an encrypted telegram in the form a tape with holes. And there's also a heading which contains the address of the recipient.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I believe you identified that for [sic] 24 hours both the tape containing the encoded telegram and the key are destroyed by fire. If --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If the key for a particular telegram is destroyed, can that tape where the telegram is written ever be decoded again?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: By what means would a signal carrying an encrypted telegram be transmitted?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: That telegram can be sent by an open or public communication means. Because it is already encoded, it doesn't have to be further protected. It can be sent by a teleprinter machine without any additional encoding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is it transmitted by radio, radio relay, or by other means?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Both radio and radio relay means. What we had was mostly radio-relay communication means and the integrated telephone means because radio relay and integrated telephone means are a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now while a telegram is being transmitted, what are the operators at both the sending and receiving side doing? Is it an automated process?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's an automatic procedure, yes. They can do other things at the same time because telegrams kept on coming constantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could someone else with the same equipment, the same device, listen in on the transmission of a telegraph, and then essentially get that telegraph and be able to decrypt and read it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me tell you that it would be somewhat hard for anybody to get a hold of all the necessary equipment to intercept such communications because our radio-relay routes went across the territory under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska, save for some routes, for example, Vlasic that went via Travnik. And even if the enemy side had managed to secure the receipt of such signals, they would not have been able to decode such a telegram. In order for them to be able to do that, they would have had to have the appropriate equipment which they could have because those equipments were left behind on the other side. They would have had to have the key as well, and the key - as the word says - is the key of everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, where did these keys come from? Where were they supplied from during the war?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: All units of the VRS, before my arrival, were supplied by the communications organ of the Main Staff of the VRS, i.e., the desk officer for cryptographic data protection, Lieutenant-Colonel Radakovic. As of March 1995 onwards, I did that. As I have already told you, those keys were produced you know where. I have to say something important. They were not mailed or sent by a third person or anything like that. They were sent by secure means and under arms protection. Let me say that all telegrams were processed, i.e., they were encoded and decoded, in a Faraday's cage that all the units of the corps rank and sometimes even brigade had. That procedure excluded any unwanted source of radiation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When you say "that procedure," are you talking about the Faraday's cage or something other?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand you, sir. What do you mean? Oh, yes, yes, we're talking about the encoding and decoding procedure. That took place in a Faraday's cage, all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to take a look at some telegrams that were sent during the time-period of July 1995. First of all, sir, can you tell me where you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we learn what a Faraday's cage is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that going to be counted against my time? Okay. I'll ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What is a Faraday's cage, sir? Could you please repeat what a Faraday's cage is.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can, of course. A Faraday's cage was named after a scientist, Faraday. He made a room or a space, in practical terms, a cage, with a lot of conduits to encapsulate all the radiation within a space without letting it out of that space. I'm referring to the electromagnetic waves that are created every time a teleprinter is switched on and starts working.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what would be the function or purpose behind operating a teleprinter within such a Faraday's cage?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The purpose is this. When a -- an original text is typed, if the enemy side would happen to have the same kind of technology and capabilities to come to a distance of 300 metres from the place where such a telegram is processed, they could receive those signals by just following the typing on the teleprinter and that's how they could obtain the contents of the open-sourced text.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then how did the Faraday's cage prevent that from happening?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The signal is lost within the conduits which enclose the wall of such a Faraday's cage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to take a look at some telegrams that were sent during the time-period of July 1995. First of all, can you tell me where you were located during the first half of July 1995?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean from the 1st to the 15th? In the month of July, I was in Crna Rijeka, save on 13th and 14th of July when I wasn't in Crna Rijeka, I was in the place I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what about the days after the 15th, how long were you at Crna Rijeka for the days after the 15th?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was there all the time. I was absent from time to time, if I needed to do something in the vicinity of that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where specifically in Crna Rijeka were you and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Goljak 1 or in the wooden huts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to look at P2109.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for the document, I can say that it's dated 11th July 1995. First of all, sir, have you seen this document before today?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have. During the preparations for this testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the last page in both languages, based on what you have just told us, would this be an act or a telegram?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your response, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Has the last 30 minutes been in vain, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could you please respond to the objection without asking further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I base it upon his prior testimony. I said: "Based on what you have just told us, would this be an act or telegram," so it is basing it back on the discussion that we had, a rather lengthy discussion, about what documents are called "acts" and what documents are called "telegrams." So I don't really know what the -- I don't know how else to phrase this question basing it on the prior testimony that we've had now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: A non-leading phrasing of the question is: What is this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then can I get a ruling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, is this that we have before us, based upon what you've described for us, would it qualify as an act or a telegram?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how we can know that it is act rather than a telegram?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's very simple. This was a written on a typewriter, not a teleprinter. It has a round stamp and there is an indication of the command that received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the initials "S.R." that are handwritten next to General Mladic's name, what would that denotation normally stand for or mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The answer to your question would be, this doesn't mean anything. When I say that it doesn't mean anything, that -- what I'm saying is this -- this was not signed by General Ratko Mladic. This is an original document, so his signature should be there if he had ever signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if an original act had a signature, is the signature itself transmitted to the receiving party to become part of the telegram received on the other end?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The original signature cannot be transmitted by telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What are the obligations of an encryptions officer receiving an original that is unsigned? What can they do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: He has to transmit it because it was brought to him by somebody who has the authority to send telegrams.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if I can look at P2125, and this will be dated 15 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you're left with about ten minutes according to our estimates. I don't know how far you are still.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at about 12 minutes, based on my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So we should be able to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is dated 15 July 1995. Based on your knowledge, was General Mladic present in Crna Rijeka at that time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, again, based upon your definitions and testimony, is this an act, original, or a telegram?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm sorry to do this to you. Could we go back to the previous document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. That would be ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, 2109. Do you perhaps need them both on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Both -- both versions. Could we see the last page, please. If you look at the original, Mr. Stevanovic, could you tell us what date that is at the bottom of -- just below the signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Below the signature, in the stamp, the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 15th of July. The English says "13th," Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ah, I did not note that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then it should be -- we should know what the correct date is, and I suppose it's the one on the original, and we will needed an amended translation uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I trust my colleagues on the other side will do that since it's their exhibit. If we can go back then to P2125.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at the upper left hand part of the document, what does the string of numbers after confidential or confidential number, I guess, is the abbreviation, what does that 04/12-302 tell you about this document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: 04/12, you mean, and the rest? Since we're talking about a radio-relay communication, this is the number that was assigned to the communications organ of the Main Staff of the VRS and he uses this number every time he sends documents to regulate cryptographic communications of the VRS. This document was created in the Main Staff of the VRS, and I know that for a fact because I worked in that department myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when you say "he uses it," who is the "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The communications organ of the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can I put another question. We see on the original after the name Ratko Mladic again this abbreviation, S.R. What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's supposed to mean "svojo rucno [phoen]," in his own hand, signed by General Mladic personally. And that is obviously not the case here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you earlier had said that General Mladic was not in Crna Rijeka on this date. Do you --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if any orders personally originating from General Mladic came to the Main Staff from him while he was wherever he was on 15 July or the day after?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: During the time-period of 14 July through 17 July 1995, did you note any orders that were sent by the Main Staff to subordinate units ordering the commission of crimes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What about incoming telegrams from subordinate units? Do you recall any that were out of the ordinary in relation to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since I usually did not read telegrams but in view of developments and throughout the war when some major developments are concerned some important combat operations, I would read some telegrams. I remember one of these telegrams. It arrived from the Zvornik Brigade and it so happened that it arrived directly to the Main Staff rather than the Drina Corps, which meant that it was just forwarded from the Drina Corps directly to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: With the signature of the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And was that the normal means of transmission of telegrams from the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was an exceptional case. The usual thing would be for a telegram from the Zvornik Brigade or any other brigade from the Drina Corps, it would have to arrive in the Drina Corps. It would have to be processed and only then with the command -- with the signature of the commander of the Drina Corps, it could only then be sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to look at P1513.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And when that comes up, sir, I'd like to have you take a moment to look at that and tell us if you recognise that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I assume it's a P number.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. P1513.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that on your list?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It was on the e-mail proofing note that was sent, I believe, Monday evening at 4.00, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at this document - and perhaps if you need the second page, please let us know - do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do. And I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What is this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the commander of the Zvornik Brigade informing the Drina Corps about the situation in his area of responsibility or, rather, the situation in the area where the 28th Division is trying to break through to Tuzla. Parts of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And -- okay.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: And -- and about what he did. That's what he speaks of.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what do you recognise this document to be, in relation to what you've been telling us?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How does this relate to the one telegram that you told us came in with the signature of Mr. Pandurevic that was done exceptionally?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the telegram, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Almost done. Last two questions. How often did you have an occasion to interact with General Mladic at Crna Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I met General Ratko Mladic on the 9th of May at Tvrdimici when he landed with General Kukanjac at the command post of the 4th Corps. From then until arriving in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, I did not see him. When arriving in the communications regiment, that is to say, Main Staff, and arriving Goljak and placing all of that under my own responsibility, from then onwards I saw him very often and I contacted with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What are your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mentioned the 4th of May. Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I mentioned the 4th of May then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, sorry -- no, it was my mistake. 9th of May. Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say exactly whether it was the 8th or 9th of May, but it was 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what are your impressions, as a career military officer, of General Mladic as a military officer?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: A highly professional officer, fair but stern. A person who does not take defeat, does not like defeat. A person who respected all peoples and exceptionally liked his own people and protected his own people. And he and his family became victims of such views and such work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If you could just explain the last part of your answer as I'm not following and I suspect others are not. When you say: "He and his family became victims of such views and such work," I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think -- I think that it is well known that Mr. Ratko Mladic during the war lost his daughter who had a degree in medicine and then he fell ill himself. No greater tragedy is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, I thank you for answering my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Are you ready for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can certainly get started. What time do we break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given the way we sat today, we planned to stop at about five to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We've covered the 15 minutes this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, do you believe that many thousands of Srebrenica sons and husbands were summarily executed shortly after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really do not know the exact number, but I do know that a certain number were executed. The exact number I really don't know. I am saying all of this in all sincerity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't ask you for the exact number. I don't know where you're getting that. Many thousands, do you believe many thousands were summarily executed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I really do apologise to you, but when you say "many thousands," it could have been 20.000 then. That's the question. I mean, I really don't want to offend you, but the question is not phrased properly. You know what "many thousands" means. I cannot give an answer that would just amount to no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Roughly how many people do you think were summarily executed by General Mladic's troops at the fall -- after the fall of Srebrenica? Just rough. Rough figure. You were in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the Main Staff, but since this is a very serious matter and one should not calculate, I do apologise, but I cannot give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: More than ten?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat: If it had to do with personal weapons I could say approximately. However, since I honour victims, my own and those of others, I cannot give just an approximate answer. I apologise once again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You won't give my any answer about the number of Srebrenica victims you believe happened?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I object. It misstates the evidence. The witness has now on three occasions answered the exact same question that keeps being posted to him by saying he cannot give a exact figure. So after the witness says "I cannot give an exact figure," to ask him three more times to give an exact figure is inappropriate and is considered badgering the witness in my jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection denied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, another chance. Do you want to give us some idea of how many victims you're willing to acknowledge, just rough, your roughest idea, as a serious officer of the VRS attached to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to object to this question as being vague. Now he has changed the question, talking about victims. Victims of what? If he is talking about something that was from direct, I would like to know what it is from direct he's talking about. If he is talking about a specific incident, he should talk about a specific incident. If he's basing it on a prior answer of a witness, he should base it on the prior answer of a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We can simplify it. Victims of summary execution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is that a question for me? I'd like to continue and finish my response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd object to his badgering the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We're getting at cross purposes, Your Honour. I think I have -- I think you get the gist of my objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- so I will hold it to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do. And I guess Mr. McCloskey's response that the victims of the executions does answer that objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, one more time. Can you give us your roughest belief of how many people were summarily executed after Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: My family upbringing, then the upbringing I received during my education and schooling does not allow me to exchange in that kind of trade. As for all the victims in Srebrenica and all others, I do not want to give mere estimates, approximations, since I really do not know what the exact figure is regarding these executions, and that is the reason I mentioned in my introduction as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, you've testified that you were away on 13 and 14 July to your birth place. You started your testimony by telling you were born in Zvornik. Were you -- were you in the Zvornik area on the 13th and 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What village?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Lijesanj, the village I was born in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what -- how close is that to the Petkovci dam?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Petkovci dam?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: About 40 kilometres. On the other side. Petkovici is after Zvornik, Lijesanj before Zvornik on the northern side, on the left bank of the Drinjaca river.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how close is to the village of Orahovac?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: Roughly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you knew when you were in Zvornik on the 13th and 14th of July that thousands of Muslim prisoners were brought up to the Zvornik area. It's a small area. You knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Never heard one word about those thousands of Muslims that were brought up and put in schools, scattered from Orahovac, Petkovci, Kuzla [phoen], Rocevic. They were at the Standard barracks in Karakaj. They drove from Kula Grad all the way up through town to all those places, you never heard one word about any Muslim prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first information about all of this, the first information, I mean, I'm speaking under oath and I'm telling the truth, the first information I received through the mass media of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm saying this in all sincerity. I did not know a thing about any of that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see on TV that was played on Serb television on the 14th horrible pictures of dead and mutilated Serbs that was being played for the public consumption on the 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR STEVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could take the break now, I'd appreciate it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, we've come to the end of the day for today. We would start again tomorrow morning at half past 9.00. But before you leave, let me just warn you that you are not allowed to speak to anybody about any part of your testimony that you have given or that you still have to give tomorrow, until you're excused from further testifying. Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may follow the usher, and we'll see you tomorrow at half past 9.00 in the same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we'll convene tomorrow morning, the 7th of May, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom. Did you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to inform -- I should be less than an hour tomorrow. I don't anticipate a lot of questions. I just wanted everyone to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. McCloskey. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 7th day of May, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.54 p.m.,
